title: GS Delivers Electric Baggage Tractors to Zhuhai Airport - Aviation Pros
content: Delivering news and insights on the issues and emerging trends shaping aviation worldwide Ground support equipment manufacturer GS has delivered electric baggage tractors and lithium-ion forklifts to Zhuhai Jinwan International Airport in China as the airport expands its ground handling capabilities. The equipment, delivered in multiple batches, includes TB30N electric baggage tractors and 5-ton lithium-ion forklifts. The vehicles will support baggage transport, cargo handling and other airport ground operations. The TB30N features a CATL lithium battery and thermal management system designed to operate in temperatures ranging from minus 30 to 60 degrees Celsius. Safety features include battery fire suppression and a tow-pin anti-disengagement device, while shock absorbers on both axles are designed to improve operating stability. The forklifts will support loading, unloading and material handling activities in cargo terminals and baggage handling areas. Following delivery, GS personnel provided training for ground handling staff covering equipment operation, routine inspections, maintenance and safety procedures. The deployment comes as Zhuhai Jinwan International Airport prepares to bring its second terminal into operation, expanding capacity at the airport in China's Greater Bay Area.

title: GS25 enters Cambodia, targets 500 stores within a decade - Mobility Plaza
content: The South Korean convenience chain has opened its first store in Phnom Penh with local master franchisee META Retail, its third overseas market after Vietnam and Mongolia. GS Retail has opened the first GS25 convenience store in Cambodia, at Olympic Stadium in Phnom Penh, under a master franchise agreement with local company META Retail. The South Korean chain aims to operate more than 500 stores in the country within 10 years. The agreement follows more than a year of market research and feasibility studies,  as reported by The Korea Times. META Retail, backed by its parent META Group, will manage the supply chain, marketing, store operations, recruitment and staff training. The first store stocks around 3,000 products, including the private-label brands Yours and Real Price, and features a café-style concept aimed at Generation Z and young professionals. Korean products make up about half of the food range, with items such as bungeoppang fish-shaped pastries, snacks, ready meals and triangular gimbap. GS25 cited Cambodia's young population, with more than 60% under 35, as a key driver for its plans. "Through close collaboration with local partners, we will introduce differentiated products and services and continuously strengthen our global business competitiveness," said Jeong Chun-ho, Executive Vice President and head of the convenience store business unit at GS Retail. Cambodia is GS25's third overseas market. The brand entered Vietnam in 2018, where it had 456 stores at the end of October, and Mongolia in 2021, where it operated 284.

title: The Best Matzo Ball Soup In Los Angeles Might Be Better Than Bubbe's - Tasting Table
content: The original Birdie G's in Santa Monica opened in 2019, and it was quickly recognized as one of the best restaurants in Los Angeles for its Jewish-American-inspired menu. When it opened, The Los Angeles Times called it "Santa Monica's hottest restaurant of the year." Later, the restaurant was named a Michelin Bib Gourmand. One of the signature dishes that earned Birdie G's all its accolades is chef Jeremy Fox's comforting yet elegant matzo ball soup, which some say is the best in the region. There are three key ingredients for traditional matzo balls: matzo meal, fat, and eggs. It's a seemingly simple dish, so what makes this matzo ball soup so special? Tasting Table spoke with chef Jeremy Fox to find out. The original Birdie G's closed at the end of 2025, but the restaurant recently reopened in Century City, bringing its beloved matzo ball soup to Los Angeles. To this day, the matzo ball soup is the dish that causes Fox the most stress because "I'm never going to beat that person's grandmother's matzo ball soup ... So I really work hard to make sure that ... the matzo ball soup is where it should be." Chef Jeremy Fox's matzo ball soup is richer and has more umami flavors than most — and he shared a lot of his matzo ball tips and tricks that make it so. First, he uses matzo meal from The Matzo Project in Brooklyn, New York, mixed with his house-rendered schmaltz, made by rendering chicken fat and onions. He told Tasting Table that the matzo meal and schmaltz are mixed with organic eggs and "lots of fresh dill," plus a little bit of baking powder. Fox takes inspiration from his grandmother's matzo ball soup, although he admittedly makes it in a different style. "Her matzo balls were very very light. Definitely floaters and ours are more sinkers," said Fox. The chicken broth, however, is labeled on the menu as "Rachael's chicken broth." It's named after Fox's wife, Rachael Sheridan, and is made using chicken backs, feet, and wings. "So it has a good amount of gelatin," he explained. After a cooking and cooling process, the stock then gets steeped with gribenes and dill stems. Fox said that enriches the stock and gives it a roasted chicken quality. The big matzo ball is served with some fresh carrots and fresh dill, and then topped with carrot miso. The stock is then poured tableside, melting the miso into the broth. From the dense yet still pillowy matzo ball to the rich chicken broth, and the umami from the carrot miso, this soup is the ultimate bowl of comfort.

title: I swapped my Apple Watch Ultra for a sub-$250 outdoor watch - here's what I gained (and lost) - ZDNET
content: Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget. Why you can trust ZDNET: ZDNET independently tests and researches products to bring you our best recommendations and advice. When you buy through our links, we may earn a commission. The GS Explorer S beats the Apple Watch SE 3 on battery, GPS and water resistance, but lacks Apple's polished user experience. Back in October 2017, I took off my Casio G-Shock for the last time, strapped on an Apple Watch Series 3, and haven’t looked back. I worked my way up through Apple’s lineup until the Ultra was released in 2022. Today, I’m wearing an Ultra 4. Also: I tested the Apple Watch Ultra 4, and these 4 upgrades matter most Given how attached I’ve become to the Apple Watch, it’s rare for me to even review any alternatives (I gave the Garmin Fenix 8 Pro a go, but it wasn’t for me), so I was surprised to find how much I liked the sub-$300 Mibro GS Explorer S Titanium, a watch from a lesser-known brand. I got to test the titanium version of the GS Explorer S, but note there’s a cheaper ceramic model that’s virtually identical except for three things — the material (titanium alloy vs. ceramic and fiber-reinforced polymer), mapping (only the titanium version has offline mapping), and of course, price. The weight is also slightly different at 0.18 oz, but that’s small enough to ignore. To keep things simple, I’m not including the titanium version with the metal band in this comparison. Another feature that’s key to the success of a smartwatch is battery life. A few things stand out to me with this watch, both positive and negative. As an Apple Watch wearer, getting a couple of days from my Ultra is good, so I find going well over a week between charges quite remarkable. It eliminates that nightly charge, which I’d appreciate on those multi-day hikes where I’d normally take my Apple Watch charger. Also: Suunto Race 3S review: How real-time dynamic pacing improved my trail runs However, I’m so used to charging my Apple Watch nightly that it’s become a ritual, and switching to a weekly (or even less frequent) charging schedule makes it more likely I’ll forget. Also, it comes with a proprietary magnetic charging cable rather than a standard USB-C, which is a little more limiting. I suppose the good news is that if I lose it, there are replacements available. I like that it comes with two bands, which gives more options. I’m a fan of orange, so that’s my choice there. And, in contrast to a lot of smartwatches, changing the band is relatively easy because it uses a custom quick-release spring bar that can be opened with a finger. Nice touch. The Corning Gorilla Glass 3 gets a thumbs-up from me, despite being over a decade old. There are much worse materials to make a smartwatch crystal from, and I expect it to resist scratches, scrapes, and bumps well. For a rugged watch, the screen is the part most likely to get scratched, and decent protection is vital if the watch is to survive for any length of time. However, it’s not invulnerable by any stretch of the imagination. And I know from experience that it won’t be anywhere near as durable as the sapphire that’s on my Apple Watch Ultra. But that’s in a totally different price category. Another thumbs-up from me is the display’s 1,500-nit brightness, making it ideal for outdoor conditions. If you’re thinking of going for the titanium model to get your hands on mapping, know that the maps are limited to 31 x 31-mile (50 x 50 km) tiles, which explains the odd number. Also, while you get features such as route following, deviation alerts, one-tap return, and track-back navigation, it lacks advanced routing features like route creation and rerouting. Also: I tried a $200 smartwatch with voice recording – it beat the Apple Watch in a few key ways The mapping is also somewhat sparse. But remember, I’m from the UK and we have excellent Ordnance Survey mapping of the entire country down to 1:25,000 resolution at an incredible level of detail. So for me, anything that doesn’t show me everything from big boulders on my path feels sparse. Compare the mapping to what I can get on my Apple Watch from the mapping service in the Outdooractive app (iOS/Android). The Mibro Fit app is somewhat hit-and-miss, but it’s nowhere near as bad as the reviews made it out to be, so I feel it’s improved over the last couple of years. Yes, it’s a bit clunky and rough around the edges, but it did the job. There’s no point bothering with an outdoor smartwatch if the data you’re gathering is inaccurate or incomplete. When reviewing outdoor gadgets, conscious of — and clear about — the fact that I’m one person, and the best I can do is compare one device against another. So, when I was testing the accuracy of the heart rate, SpO2, and location data, I compared them to the Apple Watch Ultra 4. I tested the sensors while resting, walking, and hiking, and compared the data between the two devices. Two conclusions came from my testing: This is an obvious question that a lot of people are going to be asking, but it comes down to this: the Apple Watch is the clear winner, with one big, glaring caveat. From the apps to advanced health features, optional 5G, and built-in payment handling, not to mention safety features such as fall and crash detection, the Apple Watch is better… if you have an iPhone. Also: I tested the world’s first solar AMOLED sports watch – how charging works If you have an Android, the GS Explorer S is the better smartwatch. Compare this to, say, the Apple Watch SE 3, and you get better battery life (18 hours of normal use vs. 20 days), better GPS (single-band vs. dual-band), and better water resistance (164 feet vs. 328 feet, and the GS Explorer S is OK with diving to 98 feet). And if we’re comparing the titanium model, there’s mapping (although there are also plenty of mapping apps for the Apple Watch). It leaves the SE 3 in the dust. I could compare it to the Ultra 4 and say you get a lot of outdoor smartwatch for a lot less, but it’s hard to make a fair comparison either way, given the big price difference and how mature the Apple Watch ecosystem is. If you’re an Android user, the Apple Watch ecosystem isn’t on your radar, so the field is more open since flagships like the Pixel Watch 5 or Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 lean more toward being smartwatches than rugged outdoor watches (the exception being the Galaxy Watch Ultra). Wearables have to fit into people’s style and aesthetic, and what I like might not suit you, so I like to offer some options. Here are a few alternatives you might want to check out: Watches are tough to review because they are so personal. I like big watches, but you might like small ones. I like a lot of information on the display, while you might like the bare minimum. We’re all different. What I can say about the Mibro GS Explorer S is that, for the price (which at the time of writing is $140 and $230 for the ceramic or titanium models, respectively), it’s a very good outdoor smartwatch. Also: Flipper Zero vs. Flipper One: Why the new model isn’t an upgrade If this does interest you, give thought to whether you want the ceramic or titanium version. The key difference is mapping, but I’m not fully sold on it because the map tiles are somewhat small and the routing features are limited when you’re actually on a route. Knowing this might tip you toward the ceramic model, unless you like the titanium look. If you’re a fitness enthusiast, the GS Explorer S will give you all the stats you need to keep you on track, and more, for a very good price, and a device that should give you a good few years of service. title: Are Federal Pay Raises Keeping Up With Inflation? The 15-Year Scorecard - MyFederalRetirement
content:
Financial Planning Resources for Federal & Postal Employees Federal pay raises have not kept pace with consumer prices since 2010. Compounded over 15 years, the General Schedule (GS) base raise trails the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) by about 15 points, and even the best-paid locality area is still roughly 8 points behind. The gap holds up under every major inflation measure, including the more generous ones, which matters for employees now 5 to 10 years from retiring and counting on a high-3 average salary that has not lost ground. This analysis compounds each year’s raise from 2010 and compares it with the change in the CPI-U annual average, using published pay tables from the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) and data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). It covers pay only. The retiree side, where cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) are tied to inflation by formula, is a separate question and is covered in Federal Retiree COLA’s and Inflation. A raise that takes effect in January is measured against the change in average prices from the prior year to that year. Three views of a GS raise are shown because the answer depends on where an employee works: the across-the-board (base) raise alone, the total raise in the Rest of U.S. locality area, and the total raise in Washington-Baltimore, which has one of the higher locality rates. Real change is the percentage gain or loss in purchasing power: the cumulative raise divided by cumulative price growth. A minus sign means the raise bought less at the end of the period than the starting salary did at the beginning. Only four of the 15 raises outpaced inflation in the Rest of U.S. locality area: 2015, 2020, 2023 and 2024. The 2023 and 2024 raises were the largest in decades, yet they recovered only part of what the 2021 and 2022 price surge had taken. Locality pay changes the picture in some years. In 2016, 2017 and 2019, the Washington-Baltimore total raise edged ahead of inflation while the base raise and Rest of U.S. raise did not. For the full locality tables, see the GS pay scale page and the OPM salary tables. Most federal retirees have no plan for this cost, and Medicare doesn’t cover it the way people assume. This workshop breaks down your real options, alongside everything else on your path to retirement. Get the details at a free FedImpact Workshop near you. The CPI-U is the most widely cited gauge, but it is an average across urban households, not any one person’s cost of living, and economists disagree about whether it overstates or understates real inflation. Critics of the CPI-U argue in both directions. Some say its substitution and quality adjustments understate what households pay. Others say it overstates inflation, which is why a chained version exists. Because of that dispute, the 15-year comparison was rerun against three other BLS measures. The most favorable pairing for federal employees is the chained CPI-U with Washington-Baltimore pay, and the raise still trails by about 5 points. The least favorable is the CPI-E with base pay alone, a gap of about 16 points. No combination closes the gap. The CPI-E is an experimental BLS series, not an official index, and the chained figure covers the 2010 and 2025 endpoints only. One more distinction: federal raises are set by their own legal formula, which is not tied to the CPI. The Federal Employees Pay Comparability Act (FEPCA) formula looks at private-sector pay through the Employment Cost Index, and the president or Congress can override it. The comparison above asks how raises compare with prices, not whether the formula was followed. The 2026 raise was 1.0% across the board, with no change in locality pay. Through October, prices were running about 3.5% above the 2025 average, so the 2026 raise is on track to lose about 2.4 points of purchasing power. That 2026 inflation figure is an estimate, since BLS did not publish an October 2025 index because of the lapse in appropriations, and it will be revised as the year closes. Including 2026, the 2011 to 2026 gap against the CPI-U widens to about 17 points for base pay and 15 points for Rest of U.S. locality pay. For 2027, the president’s alternative pay plan, sent to Congress on August 26, proposes no increase in General Schedule base or locality pay, with a separate 3.8% raise for law enforcement officers. The plan notes that the statutory formula would have produced a 3.1% base increase plus locality increases averaging 20.6%. That proposal is not final: on November 19, 40 unions asked Congress for a raise of at least 3.8%, Congress has not acted, and a continuing resolution runs through December 11. The executive order and OPM pay tables typically arrive in late December, and the 2027 federal pay freeze page tracks each step as it happens. Another year at 0% against even modest inflation would add to the cumulative gap. The Federal Employees Retirement System (FERS) basic annuity is based on the high-3 average salary, the highest average basic pay over any three consecutive years. A salary that has lost 15% of its purchasing power since 2010 produces a pension that replaces less of what the same job would have paid at 2010 prices. For employees within 10 years of retirement, three practical checks follow: Raises are the total percentage increases in the annual OPM General Schedule pay tables, effective in January, for the base (across-the-board) component and for two locality areas. Price change uses BLS annual-average CPI-U, with 2026 estimated from January to September data. Cumulative figures compound each year from a 2010 base. Real change equals one plus the cumulative raise, divided by one plus cumulative price growth, minus one. Pay raises for individual employees vary with grade, step and locality. Expanded support covers coins, keychains and pins, with material and presentation options for organizations LOS ANGELES, California – November 23, 2026 – GS-JJ announced an expansion of customization and design support that brings challenge coins, keychains and pins together within its offering for businesses, schools, nonprofits and community event organizers. The announcement focuses on coordinating product design, material selection and, where offered, presentation options around an organization’s branding, budget and event requirements. The products serve projects ranging from promotional giveaways to commemorative items and recognition programs. Organizations can incorporate their own artwork and event concepts, with specifications shaped by the intended audience, the setting in which items will be distributed and whether the finished products are intended for everyday use, display or presentation. The expansion concerns customization and design support across these categories, rather than the introduction of a new product line. GS-JJ’s existing product work includes coins, keychains and pins; the announced scope brings their design and specification options together for organizations planning event merchandise. Custom coins can feature organization logos, team crests, event graphics and commemorative wording. Projects include recognition ceremonies, retirement celebrations, fundraising events and organizational milestones. For organizations planning a formal presentation or display, the offering also includes coin cases, acrylic display stands and presentation boxes. These presentation choices allow a coin project to account for how recipients will receive, store or display the finished item, alongside the artwork on the coin itself. Schools, sports teams, nonprofits and community groups are among the organizations served. For custom keychains, material selection is a central part of the design process. GS-JJ offers three options: Keychain designs can include a company name, logo, tagline or event artwork. Design support accounts for artwork size, color requirements, budget and distribution plans. Applications include trade shows, expos, conferences and community events, where the compact format provides space for branding on an item intended for regular use. Custom pins support club activities, team recognition and community events. Designs can incorporate club logos, mascots, event imagery and distinctive color combinations. Pins may be worn on backpacks, jackets and hats or displayed on personal pin boards, giving organizations several ways to mark participation, shared interests or achievements. Karen Linda, Marketing Manager at GS-JJ, said the expanded offering includes design support and material and presentation options for different organizational and event requirements. In practice, those requirements vary by product. A coin prepared for a recognition ceremony may call for a presentation box or display stand. A keychain intended for conference distribution requires attention to artwork size, color and material. A club pin may center on a recognizable emblem and colors associated with its members. Across the three categories, GS-JJ’s support draws on the organization’s supplied identity and event concepts. The scope of each project is shaped by branding requirements, audience preferences and available budgets, rather than a single specification applied to every event order. GS-JJ produces custom lapel pins, keychains, challenge coins, medals and other promotional products. The company works with manufacturing partners to provide customized products for businesses, nonprofit organizations, schools, sports teams and tourism-related companies. Its services include customization and design support across its product categories. Karen Linda, Marketing Manager

title: GS E&C Teams Up to Speed Up Data Center Construction - Seoul Economic Daily
content: Builder Signs Agreement With LS Electric, LG Uplus and Honeywell Technologies GS E&C (006360.KS) is working with LS Electric, LG Uplus and Honeywell Technologies to shorten the time it takes to build data centers, the core infrastructure of the artificial intelligence era. The four companies plan to link their expertise in power, construction, integrated control and operations from the earliest stage of a project, cutting duplicated work and moving up the date services actually begin. GS E&C signed a memorandum of understanding with the three companies on the 23rd at the Grand InterContinental Seoul Parnas in Seoul's Gangnam district to build an integrated engineering system for data centers. The agreement divides data center construction into four stages — order preparation, design, system installation and integrated commissioning — and connects each company's technology and project experience across them. The partners will review power, design, construction, control and operational requirements together from the start of a project to minimize overlapping work at each stage. GS E&C will coordinate the various technologies during the system installation stage, drawing on its experience building data centers, and will provide construction technology needed throughout the project. LS Electric will review power grid and key equipment specifications at the order preparation stage and support power infrastructure technology during integrated commissioning. Honeywell Technologies will handle integrated control, security and safety, while LG Uplus will use its data center operating experience to define client requirements in detail. The four companies plan to reflect actual operating conditions from the design stage to reduce inefficiency in integrated commissioning. The goal is to move up the ready-for-service (RFS) date, the point at which a data center is prepared to deliver services. GS E&C said it will extend its existing technology partnerships across the entire data center construction process. The companies also plan to form a regular working-level committee to define each partner's role and detailed implementation plans and apply them to actual projects. "In the AI data center market, the ability to execute projects quickly has become an important competitive edge alongside reliable construction technology," a GS E&C official said. "Through this partnership, we will bring together the technology and experience of specialist companies in each field to improve efficiency in building data centers and deliver faster, more stable services to our clients." title: GS25 lands in Cambodia with 500-store goal - The Korea Herald
content:
Business GS25 lands in Cambodia with 500-store goal GS25 has opened its first store in Cambodia and aims to operate more than 500 outlets there within 10 years. Cambodia is the South Korean convenience store chain’s third overseas market, following Vietnam and Mongolia. GS Retail, which operates GS25, said Monday it had signed a nationwide master franchise agreement with Cambodian retailer Meta Retail after more than a year of local due diligence and feasibility reviews. The two companies opened the first store, the Olympic Stadium branch, in Phnom Penh on Friday. The roughly 400-square-meter outlet carries about 3,000 products, including items from GS25’s private-label brands Youus and Real Price. Korean-style products, including fish-shaped pastries, snacks, ready-to-eat meals and triangular gimbap, account for about half of the store’s food offerings. The outlet also features a cafe-style area designed to appeal to younger shoppers. Jung Chun-ho, head of GS Retail’s convenience store business unit, attended the opening ceremony alongside Meta Group Chairman Sok Bun Cheng and Meta Retail CEO Heng Sengly. “We will build on our overseas business experience in Vietnam and Mongolia and our Korean-style convenience store operating capabilities to establish a strong foothold in Cambodia,” Jung said. “Through close cooperation with our local partner, we will offer differentiated products and services and continue to strengthen our global competitiveness.” GS25 sees room for growth in Cambodia, where the population is young and convenience stores and minimarts are gaining traction. Meta Retail brings experience in supply chain management, marketing, store operations, recruitment and training. The two companies also plan to draw on the experience of Meta Retail’s parent company, Meta Group, as they expand in Cambodia. GS25 entered Vietnam in 2018 and Mongolia in 2021. As of the end of October, the chain had 740 overseas stores, with 456 in Vietnam and 284 in Mongolia. title: GS E&C Wins 1.8 Trillion Won Mokdong Redevelopment Deal - Seoul Economic Daily
content:
First 'Xi' Brand Project in Mokdong New Town
Complex to Be Reduced to 19 Buildings With Large Central Forest
More Orders Expected in Yeouido and Gwangmyeong GS E&C (006360) has been selected as the contractor for the reconstruction of the Mokdong 12 apartment complex in Seoul's Yangcheon district. With the roughly 1.8 trillion won project in hand, the builder's cumulative urban redevelopment orders this year have passed 7.3 trillion won. If it also secures large projects in Yeouido and Gwangmyeong, where contractors will be chosen late this year, its annual orders are expected to exceed 10 trillion won and reach around 11 trillion won. The Mokdong 12 reconstruction association picked GS E&C as its contractor at a general meeting held the previous day at Dongyang Mirae University in Seoul's Guro district, according to redevelopment industry sources on the 23rd. It marks the first time the company's "Xi" brand will be used in the reconstruction of Mokdong New Town, which comprises 14 complexes. The project will replace 1,860 existing apartment units at 326 Sinjeong-dong in Yangcheon district with 2,810 units across 19 buildings rising up to 41 stories, along with support and welfare facilities. Construction costs total about 1.7887 trillion won. Mokdong 12 sits near Yangcheon-gu Office Station on Seoul's subway Line 2 as well as Sintree Park and Gyenam Park, giving it both transit access and green space. GS E&C proposed "Ripplize Xi" as the complex name, combining "ripple," "luz" for light and the suffix "-ize" to evoke the beautiful transformation of light and water. Under the concept of "building a forest in Mokdong," the builder cut the number of residential buildings to 19 from the 22 in the original plan and created a large central woodland. The complex is planned with 15 themed gardens and about 3 kilometers of walking paths. It will also adopt Clima, a future-oriented climate response system. Sensor-driven flood barriers that detect weather conditions in real time and operate automatically, along with modular rainwater retention tanks, are designed to respond preemptively to extreme weather such as torrential rain, strengthening the complex's safety and the sustainability of its living environment. An "all-in-one high-end community" will offer 60 programs spanning education, exercise, relaxation and dining. Facilities include the Scala Library, all-day dining and an indoor swimming pool, as well as a 110-meter "Scala Bridge" linking three buildings and a sky lounge. GS E&C has won 5.5477 trillion won worth of redevelopment work this year, including the first district of the Seongsu strategic redevelopment zone in Seongdong district, one of the year's biggest prizes at 2.154 trillion won, and the Songpa Hanyang 2 reconstruction in Songpa district at 685.6 billion won. Adding Mokdong 12 brings the cumulative total to 7.3364 trillion won. More orders are lined up for the end of the year. GS E&C has been named preferred bidder for the reconstruction of the Eunha and Samik apartments in Yeouido, Yeongdeungpo district, worth 1.067 trillion won in construction costs, and the Haan Jugong 12 reconstruction in Gwangmyeong, Gyeonggi Province, worth 1.2622 trillion won. title: Meet G S - CanvasRebel Magazine
content: We’re excited to introduce you to the always interesting and insightful G S.  We hope you’ll enjoy our conversation with G below. This is an easy question for me as they seemed to do the important things right.  My parents were frugal, religious, charitable and open minded and very smart. They lived modestly and saved their earnings. My father was a house painter, a paint store owner and a landlord at a time when having nothing was a feasible starting point.. They raised 5 children on my father’s modest income. My mother was an excellent home maker and the bookkeeper. She even started a scrap book of my accomplishments when I was in high school.  She graduated from high school, my father, maybe the 6th grade so as to help his family. My perceptions of the past seem to fluctuate. Today, it feels like my childhood was idyllic. Tomorrow I might recall it differently. They didn’t pressure me toward a specific vocation. To be an artist was a little eccentric in my surroundings, but they were on board. They endured my many years of struggle with sympathy and maybe uncertainty but never second guessing them. They were nicely well rounded, Along with their parental accomplishments over the years, they seemed to appreciate lying around. on the sofa and watch television and not do too much. That seems to be the best of two worlds to me, and it set a template for how I could patiently navigate the complexities of being an unrealized young artist on my own. They allowed me to dream for the best, and to find the best however I evolved. I’m and artist and a musician. I come from a musical family and have drawn from early childhood and painted from age 12. I’ve definitely had my share of challenges that I would lump under “mental health”  and have struggled with isolation and loneliness for much of my adult life. My interests have distracted me and I feel I’ve benefited from these challenges as my identity and skills have grown through it.  I’ve had a a rich mix of experiences. I moved to NYC at 18, lived in poverty, alone, to learn about myself and how I fit in. I’d since lived in Colorado and now Arizona with my husband. Since working in my father’s paint store at age 12, I’ve done clerical work, retail, home health care, gardening, logging (!)  and house keeping among other thing that I probably can’t remember. I somewhat remodeled distressed homes that we bought and lived in. I was a classical guitarist for about ten years. I consider my 36 year relationship/marriage to be my greatest accomplishment. My art has evolved with varied styles. Presently, my paintings are narrative with characters and scenarios that intrigue me. I’m presently studying voice and acoustic guitar, especially enjoying “metal”. Now I’m nearing 70 years and can feel some physical and cognitive decline which I try to embrace. It’s hard to choose just one most rewarding aspect and they change over time. I’m almost 70 years old. This period of my life is revealing a welcome perspective. It causes me to think back on what motivated me as a younger artist/musician. I’ve generally been very fortunate to enjoy a special relationship with my work but I’d been often distracted by goals that may have served my ego more than my art. e.g. peer respect, appearances of societal success. Even making great art now seems a little impure as a motive. Letting go of those motives has freed me to work with an organic relation to my brain regardless of those distractions. Not easy to describe. It’s an acceptance of my limitations and finding satisfaction there. My body and my cognition are diminishing and I are now have fewer options but to enjoy the work. So, I have two vocations these days and I can move from one to the other as I choose. I’m a student of singing and rhythm guitar. Being a novice I let my specialties choose me. Presently it’s “metal”; extra fun on an acoustic guitar. I naively had no idea that there was a learning curve to this. So now, I’m 2.5 years at something I thought would take a month or two. lol. I practice for hours, perform open mics and love the respite from painting. And painting is now also better. Free of trying to create something special, I basically follow my interests and let them guide me. There’s an intellectual reward to this . An honor to pass on some insights. Perhaps vague, but the greatest value of anyone’s journey and what they “do”, is their relationship to the act.   For example, recognize and validate the things that are not you. For me, that is to find the things in my world that feel wrong, like consumption and engaging in wasteful acts. I try to have a minimal polluting impact on my world. I try to find the simplest solutions to every day acts,  to feel satisfaction in solitude and in a much reduced level of activity that is outside my needs. There’s a spiritual value to this, because if I can be freed of obligation so I can be the unique being I am. I shop less, drive less. These limitations may open up space in my mind to think and act more deeply. The “rode less traveled” is not encouraged or easy, we are conditioned to be busy and to consume. Honestly I’m not sure about all this. I have my indulgences and I shouldn’t assume to have answers that apply to everyone.  I try to recognize  when my needs and wants are designed by someone else for the profit of someone else at my expense or the expense of society. Disengaging from the societal treadmill can save one’s assets for one’s own peace. This applied to me as an artist/musician and perhaps more of us have a creative heart that they don’t indulge. I use the word “creative” here very loosely in that a person can be creative in loving their family, or friends or themselves. title: Clonin' Keys, Makin' Gs Walkthrough - IGN

Randy calls Lucia and Jason and asks them to steal a Granforma Zorrusso. This Grand Theft Auto VI Chapter 3 mission is a tutorial for a pivotal tool: the Key Cloner, and this official IGN GTA 6 guide walks you through it. This mission can be completed solo or as a pair. It’s a quick one – or at least it should be! Once you arrive at the apartment parking lot, you’ll call Randy for more information. He’ll have one of his guys send you an app for the Key Cloner. Download it, then you’re good to start hunting for the Granforma. You’ll find the red Granforma Zorrusso tucked away in the shadows on the east side of the garage. If you WAiNK It, you’ll see it sells for a whopping $23,375 and has an advanced tracker. Use the Key Cloner to get into the car. Unlocking cars with digital keys is similar to using the Slim Jim to unlock cars with physical keys. Use the right thumbstick to move around the circle until you find the weak spot, indicated by how fast the key clones and the audio cue. Hold it there and the door unlocks, allowing you to enter and drive immediately – no hotwiring required. As Randy said on the call, the only good way to deal with an advanced tracker is to drive fast. You’ll have a very brief grace period after starting the car before the advanced tracker activates. The tracker icon above the minimap begins pulsing and the circle around it fills with red as the tracker activates. Once the ring is completely filled red, the local police are notified about the car’s theft, earning you an instant two-star Wanted level. The only way to prevent activating the tracker is by moving fast, constantly. If you speed up enough as the tracker ring fills, you can cancel the alarm.
Do your best to get out of the area as fast and as safely as possible. Any damage you do to the car now reduces the payout you’ll get for delivering it in perfect condition. One of the best ways to get to Randy with the space to drive fast is by taking the highway. Drive just fast enough so the tracker isn’t getting set off, but not so fast that you can’t control the car. If you set off the advanced tracker of any car, the police respond to the location where it was set off, not where you are exactly as you drive – unless a cop spotted you as the tracker went off. Then they'll pursue you and you'll need to shake them like you would normally. As setting off a tracker only warrants a two-star Wanted level, passing into another district, county, or region puts you and the car in the clear so long as you're not being actively chased by cops. Be sure to keep moving fast, though, because the tracker can go off again if you drive too slow. Advanced tracker signals are blocked near Randy’s showroom, so I’d recommend slowing the cars as you get off the highway to avoid crashing at the last second. Pull into Randy’s garage to deliver the car and get your payment. After taking a look at the car, Randy asks you to join him over at a big whiteboard with “WANTED” written on top. He introduces a list of 15 cars a client of his wants. If you can find and bring the listed cars to Randy in top condition, you can make a lot of money.
Now when you scan cars out in Leonida, you'll get an extra notification if you find a car on Randy’s list. You can see the car list any time in the Robberies menu of the Map, under Randy’s Wish List. We also have a guide with hints on where to find each of the cars. You can talk to Randy more if you’d like, but leave when you’re ready. If you need a car, you can use one of the three branded cars for free just outside the showroom. As you leave, Randy texts you if you earned a condition bonus payment for the car you delivered. If you delivered the Granforma in perfect condition, you’ll get an extra $10,000. With this mission complete, you can now work on a new optional mission called Randy's Wish List. Check IGN's official guide page for help with these vehicles. Now that you have the Key Cloner, practically no civilian car is off limits. title: 8,502 voter applications filed at two-day SSR camps; Kolathur tops list - DT Next
content: CHENNAI: More than 8,502 physical forms were submitted across 16 Assembly constituencies in Chennai district during the two-day Special Summary Revision (SSR) camps held over the weekend, on November 21 and 22. After releasing the draft electoral roll on November 12, the Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC) organised special drives at all polling stations on November 21 and 22 to facilitate voter additions, deletions, corrections, and address changes. While 1,698 applications were received on Saturday, the turnout surged on Sunday, with the officials receiving 6,804 forms. During the drive, 5,156 new voter enrolment forms (Form 6) were submitted in bulk, followed by 3,213 requests for address shifting and corrections (Form 8), 132 applications for deletion (Form 7), and one overseas elector form (Form 6A). Among the constituencies, Kolathur recorded the highest turnout with 997 forms, followed by Perambur 751, Virugambakkam 743, Villivakkam 681, and Dr Radhakrishnan Nagar 667. The lowest was recorded in Thiru Vi Ka Nagar with 335. District Election Officer and GCC Commissioner GS Sameeran inspected the special camp at Thiru Vi Ka Higher Secondary School in Shenoy Nagar under the Anna Nagar constituency on Sunday. The next special camp will be held across all polling stations in Chennai district on Sunday, November 29, from 10 am to 5 pm.

Goldman has three operating segments: Asset & Wealth Management, Global Banking & Markets, and Platform Solutions, with the latter including transaction banking and consumer partnerships. 10 Questions About Artificial Intelligence: Part 2 Artificial intelligence (AI) has been and remains one of the fastest-growing technology developments in history. Just a few years after becoming broadly known, AI represents a significant portion of the global economy and is now the preeminent focus among investors. Developments in AI have progressed and continue to unfold rapidly, and new revelations on one day - say, the release of Meta Platforms Inc.'s Muse model - can make preconceptions about AI seem out of date.  Based on input from clients, investors, industry experts, and our own analytic team, Argus has put together what we see as 10 current key and enduring questions about AI, along with our responses. We've broken these 10 questions into Parts 1, 2, and 3.  Part 2, presented below, addresses three key questions including risks that white-hot growth at the GPU makers might slow, key adjacencies benefiting from AI infrastructure build-outs, and a discussion of companies best and worst-positioned amid AI disruption. Following publication of Part 2, we will be publishing Parts 3. We welcome feedback from clients and will continue to refine our 10 questions about AI in real time in response to this exciting and ever-changing opportunity.  QUESTION 4: At the heart of the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution are the graphics processing unit (GPU) developers, led by Nvidia Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and followed by a host of others. What is the risk that these companies' white-hot growth slows or stops? ANSWER 4: AI infrastructure investment has broadened out from an initial focus on hyperscaler data centers to a broader set of customers, including enterprises, sovereigns, and neoclouds. Wider adoption is being driven by the much more diverse range of use cases driven by agentic AI. This broadening of the market has benefited the makers of GPUs, which represent the foundational piece in massive clusters required for model training, deep learning, and inference. Nvidia is the tentpole company of the AI revolution, initially repurposing its GPU gaming cards for early AI tasks. The company was also subject to fluctuations in the crypto market and consumer cycles in gaming demand. Nvidia's revenue declined 7% in fiscal 2020, rebounded to mid-50% annual growth in FY21 and FY22, and was flat in FY23 on softening in crypto and consumer end markets. After two years of triple-digit growth in FY24 and FY25, growth moderated to 6% in FY26 before reaccelerating to 87% in the January 2027 fiscal year. Although growth is on a path to 'moderate' to the 70% range in FY28, note that growth in dollars remains robust: rising from $216 billion in FY26 to an estimated $410 billion in FY27 and to $680 billion in FY28, according to the consensus. If not for supply constraints, according to CEO Jensen Huang, FY28 top-line growth would be meaningfully higher. Nvidia has teamed up with Wall Street giants (Apollo Global Management Inc., Blackrock Inc., Goldman Sachs Group Inc., and others) to raise $500 billion in capital for AI infrastructure. Nvidia anticipates multiple years of strong growth ahead. AMD is No. 2 in GPUs and is also benefiting as inference drives demand for industry standard servers (ISSs) using AMD's central processing units (CPUs). AMD generated $6.6 billion in revenue in 2010 but did not get back above that number until 2019. After three years of mid-double-digit growth in 2020-22, revenue declined in 2023 and grew 14% in 2024. Fueled by both its CPU and GPU franchises, growth accelerated to 34% in 2025 and is on a path to accelerate from 47% in 2026 to 73% in 2027. In dollar terms, AMD's revenue is forecast to rise from $35 billion in 2025 to $51 billion in 2026 and $88 billion in 2027. Companies including Broadcom Inc. and Marvell Technology Inc., which make application accelerators and XPUs (both of which are task-specific GPUs), are reporting similar growth trajectories as customer and market opportunities broaden. AI infrastructure spending grew about 60% annually to $320 billion in 2025, according to industry analysis firm IDC. AI infrastructure spending is on a path to exceed $1 trillion in 2029, the firm estimates. IDC noted that AI infrastructure investment is accelerating at a pace that signals a clear shift away from experimentation to a sustained, multiyear capital commitment cycle by end customers. Based on these and other forecasts and guidance from the major GPU providers, we expect GPU and related semiconductor growth to sustain and in many cases accelerate from high levels in coming years. QUESTION 5: What are some the key adjacencies that are benefiting from AI development? And which of these companies are best positioned to thrive? ANSWER 5: The initial gold-rush phase of AI was characterized by intense activity among hyperscalers to build massive GPU clusters and support infrastructure as they sought to develop and train their own large language models (LLMs). But this focus on AI data centers also represented one of the key bottlenecks in AI infrastructure. AI content, in the words of rock singer Meat Loaf, was 'all revved up with no place to go.' Late in 2024 and early in 2025, Argus noted that the AI revolution had primarily been focused within hyperscalers (major cloud service providers) and was concentrated in GPU compute at massive cloud data centers. Argus forecast that in coming years, the AI revolution would spread out from this initial concentration at hyperscalers to include customers in other categories including major enterprises, sovereigns, and neoclouds. We further forecast that the need to accommodate AI-generated data would trigger massive business growth at data storage and memory companies. And we forecast that the need to disseminate AI data to these new classes of customers would trigger massive business growth at data networking companies.  Those forecasts began to play out during 2025, as data storage and memory companies had huge business growth and were among the best stocks in the S&P 500. During 2026, data networking companies have reported strong double-digit growth rates, and their stocks are leading the Information Technology sector and broad market. The first phase of generative AI, dominated by the training of LLMs, is giving way to the age of agentic and physical AI, which requires much more compute-intensive inference in multimodal and frontier models. This is further contributing to AI-related data growth.  Technology segments benefiting from the need to deliver AI-as-a-system include data storage and memory, networking, and traditional enterprise infrastructure. In these segments, Argus has identified multiple companies best positioned to benefit from the broadening in AI demand. In the networking space, Argus favors optical-networking leader Ciena Corp., 'cloud titan' network provider Arista Networks Inc., and enterprise industry leader Cisco Systems Inc. as three companies well positioned to deliver AI services to customers. In the data storage and memory space, Argus favors Seagate Technology Holdings plc and Western Digital Corp., which form a duopoly in nearline hard disk drives for AI data centers; Sandisk Corp. in the nonvolatile memory space; and Micron Technology Inc., the leading U.S.-based provider of DRAM and NAND memory. Data storage systems providers including NetApp Inc. are subject to higher input costs for their solutions, but NetApp has driven revenue acceleration with successful cost pass-alongs and higher prices.  Dell Technologies Inc. is a good example of the fast-developing market opportunity in the legacy enterprise infrastructure space. As of mid-2026, Dell had thousands of customers for its AI servers and related IT infrastructure including storage arrays, industry standard servers, and networking gear. None of these customers included the major hyperscalers.  As of August 2026, Dell expected at least $74 billion in AI-optimized server revenue in FY27, almost triple the $25 billion in FY26. Dell's traditional x86-based ISS revenue grew more than 120% annually in the most recent quarter. In 1H27, Dell generated as much revenue from ISS and networking than it generated in any full prior year in company history.  Outside the Information Technology sector, industrial companies providing power, cooling, electrical, and related solutions are also experiencing extraordinary growth. Top beneficiaries include Caterpillar Inc., Emerson Electric Co., Honeywell International Inc., Rockwell Automation Inc., and others. As AI demand continues to broaden out, we expect strong and even accelerated growth for providers of the adjacent infrastructure enabling the AI revolution.   QUESTION 6: Which incumbents are most vulnerable to AI disruption? And which are best positioned to integrate AI defensively? ANSWER 6: The AI revolution has been so consistently strong and inclusive that it initially swept along much of the Information Technology sector. But as the AI revolution moves beyond year three, several significant developments have revealed risks to industry incumbents across the technology landscape. These developments primarily relate to AI displacement and the impact of soaring component costs in a supply-constrained environment. Fears of AI displacement have been mainly centered in the enterprise application software space. The trajectory of these fears is expressed in the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV). The software ETF hit an all-time closing high around 117 in September 2025. The release of certain highly capable frontier models, most notably Anthropic PBC's Claude Code, showed that many formerly proprietary software tasks could be done quickly and cheaply with AI. IGV declined gradually into year-end 2025 and then its decline accelerated in the new year, reaching bottom at a closing low of 74 in April 2026. IGV has since rebounded to a low-100s level, as software companies counter displacement fears by highlighting their proprietary products, deep customer engagements, and defense against 'weakest link' cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Component prices and particularly memory prices have soared due to voracious hyperscaler appetites for hardware to support infrastructure investment. Companies with high personal computer exposure such as HP Inc. report that memory is now up to 70% of the bill of materials cost of building a PC. In releasing its newest iPhone family in September 2026, Apple Inc. raised iPhone prices by approximately $100 per device and more for high-memory-content phones. These rising costs and the urgency to invest in AI are causing chief information officers to reshape their IT budgets in some cases away from long-standing customers.  International Business Machines Corp., which in April 2026 warned of a decline in 2Q26 infrastructure revenue, reported a steeper-than-expected demand decline in July 2026. Customers shifted purchases away from IBM's mainframe computers and its complementary transactional software stack. These customers redirected spending to ISS servers, a market in which IBM no longer competes, and data storage in order to secure supply-constrained IT hardware ahead of further price increases. IBM shares declined sharply on the 2Q26 revenue miss and are down 22% year-to-date. But the stock is up sharply from pre-AI days. IBM Watson playing Jeopardy against a past champion helped popularize the concept of AI years before ChatGPT. IBM, like the software companies and makers of AI PCs, should ultimately benefit from positioning within the AI ecosystem. We expect creative disruption to continue to challenge industry incumbents.  As to which companies are best positioned to integrate AI defensively, no company is in a position to sit on the sidelines and watch its competitors bring AI practices into their everyday operations and into customer interactions. Market sectors at the forefront of AI adoption, for both offensive and defensive reasons, include Healthcare, Information Technology, and Financial. Even in regulated sectors such as Utilities, which would seem to have less urgency to integrate AI into their operations, sector companies are adding smart meter technology and using AI to upgrade their internal operations. In short, nearly every company inside and outside of the AI ecosystem will need to integrate AI both offensively and defensively. title: 2026 BMW F450 GS Trophy Review - Auto Trader NZ
content: If you don’t already know, the ‘GS’ suffix that BMW Motorrad attaches to its adventure models stands for ‘Gelände Strasse’, roughly ‘off-road/on-road’ in German. It highlights the compromise all adventure bike manufacturers must make when designing a new model. Do they make it more rideable in ‘Gelände’ riding scenarios, or do they retain more of its performance during ‘Strasse’ applications? For, as any ute owner who has fitted big mud-slinging treads already knows, upping drivability for the times when the vehicle is off-road always compromises refinement and the on-road dynamics when back in the bosom of civilisation. Which is why BMW began swapping the 21-inch front wheel of the original 1980 R80 GS for a smaller 19-inch hoop on 21st-century GS models. The 19-incher quickens the steering and makes riding on a winding sealed road more engaging; it’s more in line with the GS ethos than the larger front hoop fitted to dedicated off-road motorcycles. Despite the howls of some YouTubers who consider a 21-inch front to be a requisite component of an adventure bike, BMW has stuck a 19 to the new F450 GS. Chapeau, it’s a choice I applaud. This proves that BMW wanted to draw the line between the two contrary GS riding statements right down the middle with the F450 GS. This 178kg bundle of all-terrain riding fun is sampled here in the range-topping $14,490 Trophy variant that adds the snazzy paint scheme, a beefy bashplate, extra suspension adjustment, an extra riding mode targeted at extreme off-road use, and a clever auto-clutch so that the engine never flames out during a rocky river crossing. All these extras, except perhaps the motorsport-inspired paint scheme, enhance performance on the ‘Gelände’ side of the mission statement. An F450 GS Trophy, for me, almost represents the perfect balance of the two diverse design briefs. It would be even closer to perfect if the bike was equipped with some cross-spokes and 50/50 tyres instead of cast alloy wheels and 80/20 rubber biased towards road use. Be warned that such an upgrade is likely to add $2000 to the purchase price. BMW first surprised us with a ‘baby GS’ ten years ago when it released the underwhelming single-cylinder G310 GS in collaboration with its Indian manufacturing partner, TVS. The good news is that TVS and BMW have now built us a new twin-cylinder GS with what feels like twice the horsepower. If only this had been the ‘baby GS’ model that they released ten years ago. This time, BMW hasn’t held back on the new technology it’s incorporated into the new 450. There’s a new 420cc parallel twin with an innovative 135-degree crankshaft. That brings a new inline twin-cylinder engine sound into a segment where Chinese twins favour 270-degree cranks because their aural signature mimics that of V-twins and Japanese twins use 180-degree cranks because they rev more freely. It would be more accurate to call this new engine a 225-degree parallel twin. The piston of one cylinder reaches Top Dead Centre (TDC) when the crankshaft has rotated 135 degrees, while the other does the same when the crank reaches 225 degrees of rotation. Calling it a 225-degree crankshaft positions the new layout nicely between the 180-degree and 270-degree twins of the competition. This accurately describes how this lively new engine feels and sounds. It emits a more entertaining exhaust signature than a 180-degree twin and is keener to rev out than a 270-degree motor. Again, Chapeau, BMW. Next up, the ERC automatic clutch that’s standard equipment on the most expensive F450 GS, and optional on the other two variants of the range. Backed up by a rapid-fire quick-shifter for the six-speed gearbox, the ERC is a brilliant bit of kit and rivals the e-clutch system Honda now fits to the latest Transalp 750. The rpm point at which the ERC engages is set a bit higher than the Honda at 2700rpm, but you soon get used to it. Fast getaways are triggered by a quick twist of the throttle to wide open, and the F450 GS launches so sweetly that it’s hard to imagine any hand operation of the clutch lever being so devastatingly effective. Low-speed manoeuvres are a doddle and it’s easy to trickle the bike over gnarly obstacles off-road. Meanwhile, BMW retained the clutch lever on the left side of the handlebar so that a quick flick of it can initiate a wheelstand when required. The light, easy-to-ride dynamics are a highlight of the F450 GS Trophy experience.  As a Learner-Approved Motorcycle the engine is restricted, but a fully-fuelled weight that’s around 20kg less than some rival twins makes the BMW feel one of the friskier rides in the segment. There’s decent torque available in the middle of the rev range, making highway cruising feel relaxed and sustainable, along with the comfortable, if narrow, seat. At around 7000rpm, there’s an extra kick forward that’s easy to target with the quick-shifter.  Memories of the lethargic G310 GS fade to insignificance when riding the F450 GS. The engine performance is matched by that of the chassis. There’s none of the top-heaviness that blights the handling of some welterweight ADVs and it feels beautifully balanced, both front to rear and top to bottom. Capping it off are the quality suspension and brakes. The former makes the most of the modest 180mm of wheel travel, the firm springs prevent bottoming out on the big hits, and robust damping keeps the springs under control. Helped by radial caliper mounts and braided brake lines, the single front disc produces a stopping performance that’s arguably segment-leading. Want the rest of the stuff fitted to the Trophy but not the ERC, the fancy paint, nor the alloy bashplate? Buy the $13,890 Sport version of F450 GS. Sitting at the bottom of the F450 GS range is the $13,490 Exclusive, which is still a well-equipped bike by lightweight ADV standards despite the entire range lacking cruise control. For it comes with BMW’s easy-to-read 6.5-inch TFT screen and the brand’s brilliant switchgear. There’s IMU-enhanced traction control and ABS Pro, a decent selection of riding modes (minus Enduro Pro), adjustable hand levers, and a USB-C socket. Excellent ergonomic tailoring is a feature of all three models. The seat height might look a bit daunting on paper at 845mm, but in practice it’s an easy bike to swing a leg over. Buy the Sport to get arguably the most value in the new F450 GS range, but don’t sweat the decision too much. Any of these three models makes a mighty fine ‘baby GS’. $14,490  / 3.8L/100km  /  88g/km0-100 km/h 5.7sEngine  420cc  parallel twinMax power  36kW@8750rpmMax torque  43Nm@6750rpmDrivetrain Six-speed, chain driveWeight (claimed)  178kg

title: Forget The BMW GS — This ADV Gives You Most Of What Matters - Top Speed
content: The big BMW GS is the undisputed leader of the full-size adventure class, dominating sales with decades of updates, massive road presence, and class-setting electronics. Buyers flock to the German flagship because it eats up cross-country miles while projecting serious status at every stop. However, that prestige carries steep initial pricing and expensive dealer service bills, putting it out of reach for riders who prioritize high-mileage dependability over badge appeal. The real question is whether you actually need to spend that kind of money for serious adventure riding. The Suzuki V-Strom 1050DE proves that you can forget the BMW GS and still get most of what actually matters for long-distance travel at a lower price. Its proven 1,037 cc V-twin engine and steel frame skip the dizzying electronic complexity of expensive European rivals, but that straightforward foundation delivers the exact substance you need out in the boondocks: great torque, predictable handling, and bulletproof mechanical longevity. By offering real cross-country competence, distinct character, and rock-solid reliability for a fraction of the cost, Suzuki skips the marketing hype entirely and gives riders everything that actually counts from the GS’s arsenal. That value-first philosophy becomes even clearer when you put its sticker price next to Munich’s flagship. The big V-Strom range starts at $15,699, but that is for the base model with alloy wheels. The 'DE' signifies its off-road intentions, and you get a spoke rim combination with tires more compatible with the dirt. This model has a base price of $16,649. There's no question that the R 1300 GS is the adventure bike benchmark, but it also asks for a lot more money for its modern features like Bluetooth, navigation, and electronic suspension, and shaft drive. The base model costs $20,395, and when you start adding options and accessories to it, you are sucked into the world of BMW's packages. It will very easily drive the price up to $25,000. In effect, the Suzuki offers most of what the BMW has to offer, but at nearly half the price. Suzuki has stuck with a V-twin engine for the V-Strom 1050DE, and this is one of the coolest examples of that engine layout. This is a 90-degree V-twin that displaces 1,037 cc, has liquid cooling, and a DOHC setup. It is a short-stroke design with a compression ratio of 11.5:1 to produce 107.4 horsepower at 8,500 RPM and 73.7 pound-feet of torque at 6,000 RPM. This V-twin does not have best-in-class power figures, but it generates most of its performance low in the rev range. For an adventure motorcycle, that is incredibly good news. The result will be lower stress and therefore better longevity and better fuel economy. It is mated to a six-speed gearbox with an assist and slipper clutch that also has hydraulic actuation. The V-Strom 1050DE chooses an old-school chassis that matches its Honda-like reliability with BMW touring comfort. This is an aluminum twin-spar frame, which is expensive to produce and heavier than the frames other adventure bikes use today, but the flip side is that the V-Strom 1050 offers some of the best feel and feedback among the competition. The suspension is provided by KYB: 43 mm inverted forks with 6.7 inches of travel and a link-type rear shock with 6.6 inches of travel. Both ends are fully adjustable. The brakes consist of twin 310 mm front discs with radial four-piston fixed Tokico calipers and a 260 mm rear disc with a Nissin single-piston caliper. These are linked brakes, which is a great feature at the price. It uses spoked rims with a 21-inch front and 17-inch rear, where you'll find one of the V-Strom's quirks: only the rear rim is tubeless. The V-Strom 1050DE is 94 inches long with a height of 59.3 inches. The seat height is 34.6 inches, and the ground clearance is 7.5 inches. It has a wheelbase of 62.8 inches, weighs 554 pounds wet, and the fuel tank can hold 5.3 gallons of fuel. These are the dimensions of a normal full-size adventure motorcycle. The seat height and ground clearance are normal for the segment, while the wheelbase is a little long for the segment, which should make it very stable at speed. That is added to by its weight. All said and done, this is a very comfortable two-up tourer that feels built for riders over 60, but don’t expect it to change direction with as much ease as the competition. The V-Strom 1050DE offers just enough features to make it an enjoyable premium experience, but it does not go overboard since V-Strom owners don't care about fancy gadgets. It leads with the five-inch TFT display, but it leaves out Bluetooth and navigation. The engine has a by-wire throttle with three ride modes, cruise control, and switchable cornering traction control. Of course, the brakes might be linked, but the rear ABS can be switched off as well. The standard equipment includes a center stand, the aluminum skid plate, the engine crash bar, and a tool-adjustable windscreen. The options list includes a taller touring windscreen, the quick-release screen adjustment kit, upper crash bars, and hard or soft luggage. We want to hear from you. title: A-G’s directive on suspects’ rights must translate into action, not just promises – Sulemana Braimah - MyJoyOnline
content: The Executive Director of the Media Foundation for West Africa (MFWA), Sulemana Braimah, has cautioned that the Attorney-General’s directive on protecting the rights of arrested persons must be backed by effective enforcement to produce meaningful results. He said although the directive reinforces important constitutional and legal safeguards, its success would depend on whether law enforcement agencies translate the requirements into their daily operations. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, November 21, Mr Braimah welcomed the directive, describing decisions aimed at promoting and protecting people's rights as fundamental. However, he questioned why law enforcement agencies had, over the years, failed to consistently uphold requirements that were already captured in existing laws. The Attorney-General's directive requires law enforcement and investigative agencies, including the Ghana Police Service, the Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO), the National Intelligence Bureau (NIB) and the Narcotics Control Commission (NACOC), to comply with the constitutional 48-hour detention limit and other safeguards protecting suspects. It also requires arrested persons to be informed of the reasons for their arrest and their right to legal representation, while prohibiting the use of arrest and detention to recover civil debts, unlawful searches, torture and coercion. The agencies are further required to respect suspects' right to silence and ensure that confessions are voluntary, while submitting quarterly compliance reports to the Attorney-General detailing arrests, releases, court appearances and alleged rights violations. Mr Braimah said the directive was a welcome development but warned against allowing it to become another official declaration that generates public expectations without producing tangible changes. “The challenge is whether or not it is going to be one of those usual things where nice policy statements are made, nice declarations and directives are issued and at the end of the day we are just back to square one,” he said. He argued that the real achievement would be seen when citizens begin to experience improved protection of their rights in their dealings with law enforcement agencies. Drawing a comparison with political party manifestoes, he said governments often presented attractive promises and policies but failed to deliver the expected changes after assuming office. Mr Braimah therefore maintained that the Attorney-General's directive should be judged by its practical outcomes rather than the announcement itself. He also acknowledged that enforcing the requirements could prove more difficult in practice than it appeared on paper, making sustained commitment from the affected institutions essential. He stressed that while the directive deserved recognition, meaningful acknowledgement would only be justified when its implementation began to produce visible results for the protection of citizens' rights.
